intro:
Paul writes Philippians around AD 62 from Roman imprisonment to the first church he planted in Europe (Acts 16). This is his warmest letter—full of joy despite his chains and their hardships. The Philippians have sent Epaphroditus with financial support, and Paul writes to thank them, update them on his situation, and address some issues: unity threats from selfish ambition and a warning about Judaizers.

Philippi was a Roman colony with proud military veterans. Paul uses citizenship language: 'Our citizenship is in heaven.' The church includes Lydia (wealthy merchant), a jailer, and possibly slave girl from Acts 16—showing cross-class unity. Now some division threatens, possibly between two women, Euodia and Syntyche.

Paul doesn't command but appeals through Christ's example of humility and service. The famous 'Christ hymn' (2:5-11) shows Jesus emptying Himself, becoming obedient to death—the pattern for their relationships. Paul models contentment in all circumstances, having learned the secret of being satisfied in Christ alone.
outro:
Paul concludes with repeated thanks for their gift, assurance that God will supply their needs, and final greetings. The letter radiates affectionate partnership between apostle and church.

Philippians became a handbook for Christian joy amid suffering. Written from potential death sentence, it shows how the gospel redefines circumstances—imprisonment advances the gospel, suffering fellowship with Christ, death gain. Its call to unity through humility continues to challenge individualistic Christianity.

This letter demonstrates how gospel partnership works across distances and difficulties. The Philippians' financial support wasn't charity but investment in gospel work, and Paul's transparency about his needs models mutual dependency in Christ's body.
